questions.question_text: To graph $y = 3x + 4$, which point do you plot first?

options.why: Used the gradient as the starting point instead of the $y$-intercept.
Plotted the intercept on the $x$-axis; the $y$-intercept has $x = 0$.
Changed the sign of the $y$-intercept, which is $+4$.

questions.solution_text:
Plot the $y$-intercept first. The constant is $c = 4$.
$(0, 4)$

questions.question_text: To graph $y = 2x - 5$, which point do you plot first?

options.why: Used the gradient $2$ as the $y$-intercept instead of the constant $-5$.
Swapped the coordinates of the $y$-intercept; its $x$-coordinate must be $0$.
Dropped the negative sign of the $y$-intercept.

questions.solution_text: Plot the $y$-intercept first. The constant is $c = -5$, so plot $(0, -5)$.

questions.question_text:
To graph $y = \frac{3}{4}x + 1$, from the $y$-intercept you move right $4$.
How far up do you move?

options.why: Used the denominator; the numerator gives the rise.
Used the $y$-intercept as the rise instead of the gradient.
Did not scale the rise to match a run of $4$.

questions.solution_text:
The gradient is $\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{3}{4}$: a run of $4$ goes with a rise of $3$.
$3$

questions.question_text:
To graph $y = -2x + 5$, from the $y$-intercept you move right $1$.
What do you do next?

options.why: Dropped the negative sign of the gradient, so stepped up instead of down.
Used the $y$-intercept $5$ as the rise instead of the gradient $-2$.
Used the $y$-intercept $5$ as the rise and also dropped the negative sign.

questions.solution_text:
The gradient is $-2 = \frac{-2}{1}$: a run of $1$ goes with a rise of $-2$, so move down $2$.
Down $2$.

questions.question_text: What is the $y$-intercept of the graph of $y = 4x$?

options.why: Used the gradient as the intercept; there is no constant term.
Used the gradient coefficient $4$ as the $x$-coordinate of an intercept instead of identifying the $y$-intercept $(0, 0)$.
Plotted the gradient step instead of the starting point.

questions.solution_text:
There is no constant term, so $c = 0$.
$(0, 0)$

questions.question_text:
To graph $y = \frac{1}{3}x - 2$, from the $y$-intercept you move up $1$.
How far right do you move?

options.why: Used the numerator; the denominator gives the run.
Used the $y$-intercept as the run instead of the gradient.
Did not scale the run to match a rise of $1$.

questions.solution_text:
The gradient is $\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{1}{3}$: a rise of $1$ goes with a run of $3$.
$3$

questions.question_text: What is the first point you plot to graph $y = -x - 4$?

options.why: Dropped the negative sign on the $y$-intercept.
Plotted on the $x$-axis; the $y$-intercept has $x = 0$.
Used the gradient $-1$ as the intercept.

questions.solution_text:
Plot the $y$-intercept first. The constant is $c = -4$.
$(0, -4)$

questions.question_text:
Which graph shows the line $y = \frac{3}{2}x - 1$?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=7cm,height=7cm,axis equal image,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-4,xmax=4,ymin=-5,ymax=5,xtick={-3,-2,-1,1,2,3},ytick={-4,-3,-2,-1,1,2,3,4},grid=major,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,blue,<->,domain=-2.6666666667:4,samples=2]{3*x/2-1};\addplot[thick,red,dashed,<->,domain=-4:2.6666666667,samples=2]{3*x/2+1};\addplot[thick,green!60!black,dotted,<->,domain=-4:4,samples=2]{2*x/3-1};\node[right,blue,fill=white,inner sep=1pt] at (axis cs:3,3.5){$A$};\node[left,red,fill=white,inner sep=1pt] at (axis cs:2,4){$B$};\node[right,green!60!black,fill=white,inner sep=1pt] at (axis cs:3,1){$C$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Changed the intercept from $-1$ to $+1$ while keeping the gradient $\frac{3}{2}$.
Swapped the rise and run, using gradient $\frac{2}{3}$ instead of $\frac{3}{2}$.

questions.solution_text:
Plot the $y$-intercept $(0, -1)$. The gradient is $\frac{3}{2}$, so move right $2$ and up $3$ to $(2, 2)$, then rule the line through both points.
Graph $A$ shows this line.

questions.question_text:
Which graph shows the line $y = 2x - 2$?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=6cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-5,xmax=5,ymin=-6,ymax=6,xtick={-4,-2,2,4},ytick={-4,-2,2,4,6},minor x tick num=1,minor y tick num=1,grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,blue,<->,domain=-2:4,samples=2]{2*x-2};\addplot[thick,red,dashed,<->,domain=-4:2,samples=2]{2*x+2};\addplot[thick,green!60!black,dotted,<->,domain=-4:2,samples=2]{-2*x-2};\node[blue] at (axis cs:3.6,3){$A$};\node[red] at (axis cs:1.4,5){$B$};\node[green!60!black] at (axis cs:-3.4,4.2){$C$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Same gradient, but this line crosses the $y$-axis at $+2$, not $-2$.
Correct intercept, but this line slopes down, so its gradient is $-2$.

questions.solution_text:
The line has $y$-intercept $(0, -2)$ and gradient $2$ (rising, right $1$ up $2$).
Only line $A$ crosses at $-2$ and rises.
$A$

questions.question_text: Which way does the graph of $y = -3x + 1$ slope?

options.why: Ignored the negative gradient; positive gradients rise.
A horizontal line needs gradient $0$, but here it is $-3$.

questions.solution_text:
The gradient is $-3$, which is negative.
A negative gradient slopes down from left to right.
